question: What is the double haul in fly casting?
answer: The double haul is a line acceleration technique where the line hand pulls the fly line on both the back cast and the forward cast — distributing the workload between both hands and dramatically increasing line speed. It was introduced to the world by Marvin Hedge in 1934 when he broke the fly casting distance record by 22 feet. It is not just a distance technique — a properly timed double haul improves accuracy, loop control, and efficiency on every cast.

question: How do I learn the timing of the double haul?
answer: The fastest method is pantomime — practicing the haul motion with no rod or line in hand. Mel Krieger originated this approach in the mid-1970s teaching the Fenwick Fly Casting Schools, achieving results in under 10 minutes. Practice the down-up motion of the line hand repeatedly until the timing becomes automatic before adding the rod. Mac Brown's animated GIF on the double haul page at macbrownflyfish.com illustrates the correct sequence.

question: When should the haul begin during the casting stroke?
answer: The haul should begin around the halfway point through the casting stroke. Starting too early reduces the rod load benefit. Starting too late creates a jerky, disconnected cast. Think of the haul, the rod stop, and the rod unbend occurring simultaneously at the completion of the stroke — the synchronicity of all three is what produces maximum line speed with minimum effort.

question: Does the double haul help with short casts or just distance?
answer: Both — and most anglers underestimate how much the double haul improves short game casting. A properly timed haul produces tighter loops, better accuracy, and reduced false casting at any distance. It also protects fine tippets by allowing the same line speed with significantly less rod hand force. Every fly caster benefits from learning the double haul regardless of the distances they fish.

question: What is a single haul in fly casting?
answer: A single haul is a pull on the fly line with the line hand on only one casting stroke — either the back cast or the forward cast, but not both. Most anglers apply it on the forward cast because that is typically the delivery stroke and the direction requiring the most line speed for shooting additional line toward the target.

question: What is the rubber band drill for learning the double haul?
answer: The rubber band drill attaches a large rubber band to both index fingers to practice the double haul motion without a rod. As the hands pull apart during the haul, the rubber band creates resistance — and on the return, it reminds the line hand to come back to the ready position. The most common double haul error is failing to return the line hand to the starting position after the haul, and this drill corrects it automatically.

question: How do I test whether I have mastered the double haul?
answer: Cast using a horizontal rod plane just inches above the ground and try to keep the fly line from touching the grass. If the line hits the ground repeatedly, the timing or haul length is off — return to the pantomime drill and rebuild the motion slowly. This horizontal plane test exposes timing errors that a standard vertical cast can hide, making it one of the most effective self-diagnostic tools in fly casting.

question: What is shooting line in fly casting and when does it happen?
answer: Shooting line is the release of additional fly line through the guides after the haul — allowing the unrolling loop to carry extra line toward the target and dramatically increasing distance. It occurs either at the completion of the rod stop or just before, depending on the caster. Mastering the shoot eliminates the need for multiple false casts and allows a single back cast followed by one delivery cast for most presentations.

question: Can shooting line timing affect the shape of a presentation cast?
answer: Yes — shooting line early or late changes the layout of the cast. Shooting line late during a positive curve cast produces a question mark layout in the line rather than the standard 90-degree curve. This level of control over shooting line timing is an advanced skill that expands the range of presentation casts available on the water, particularly for reaching fish behind obstacles or in complex currents.
